title: Free characteristic criterion and normal crossings boundary
statement: Let $(X,M)$ be a locally Noetherian log regular fs log scheme [def-trf-fs-log-blowup, pqf-def-locnoeth] and let $U$ be its triviality locus. For every geometric point $\bar x$ above $x\in X$, the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular if and only if $\overline M_{\bar x}\cong\mathbf N^r$ for some finite $r\geq0$. If these equivalent conditions hold everywhere, then $X$ is regular [def-weil-regular-scheme], $U$ is open dense in $X$, and $D=(X\setminus U)_{\rm red}$ [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction] is an effective Cartier divisor: locally its ideal is generated by a non-zero-divisor [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Etale locally [def-weil-etale-morphism] at each point $D$ is cut out by a product of distinct members of a regular system of parameters. This is a normal crossings divisor, allowing the empty divisor and allowing self-intersections of its global components.

source.place: Expose VI, 1.4 and 1.7, printed pp. 69--70; Expose VIII, 3.4.4, printed p. 110, and 4.1.1, printed p. 117. Normal crossings here is the etale-local parameter criterion, not strictness of global components.

proof.text: Fix $\bar x$ above $x$. Put $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, $A=R^{\mathrm{sh}}$, $P=\overline M_{\bar x}$, $r=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbf Z}P^{\mathrm{gp}}$, and $I=(\alpha(M_{\bar x}\setminus A^\times))$. The sharp-chart lemma supplies a chart by $P$, and strict henselization is Noetherian since $R$ is. By log regularity, $A/I$ is regular and, writing $s=\dim(A/I)$, we have $\dim A=s+r$. The chart identifies the log stalk with $P\oplus A^\times$, so $I$ is generated by the chart images of $P\setminus\{0\}$.

source.place: VI, 1.2 and 1.6, printed pp. 69--70; sharp chart and log regular dimension formula.

proof.text: Choose a finite generating set $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ of the sharp integral monoid $P$, minimal under deletion, excluding $0$. Each $p_i$ is indecomposable: if $p_i=q+q'$ with both summands nonzero, expand $q,q'$ in the generators. If the expansion does not use $p_i$ then $p_i$ was redundant. If it uses $p_i$, cancellation gives a sum equal to $0$; sharpness forces every summand to be $0$, leaving exactly one copy of $p_i$, which is incompatible with both $q,q'$ being nonzero. Thus the $p_i$ are exactly the indecomposable nonzero elements, since any nonzero sum with at least two terms is decomposable. Also $P^{\mathrm{gp}}$ is torsion free: if $ng=0$, saturation puts both $g$ and $-g$ in $P$, and sharpness gives $g=0$.

source.place: VI, 1.6, P is fs sharp; elementary consequences of finiteness, integrality, saturation and sharpness.

proof.text: Write $a_i=a(p_i)\in A$. They generate $I$. None is in the ideal generated by the others: contraction of the monoid ideal $\bigcup_{j\ne i}(p_j+P)$ would give $p_i=p_j+q$, contradicting indecomposability and distinctness. Their images therefore form a basis of $I/\mathfrak m_AI$. Indeed they span, and a linear dependence over the residue field has a nonzero coefficient; deleting the corresponding vector leaves a spanning family, which by Nakayama would generate $I$ and contradict irredundance. Hence $\dim_{\kappa(A)}I/\mathfrak m_AI=n$.

source.place: VIII, Lemma 3.4.3, printed p. 110; apply monoidal ideal contraction, then ordinary Nakayama to the finite ideal I.

proof.text: Suppose $A$ is regular, of dimension $d$. Since $A/I$ is regular, the regular-quotient kernel lemma gives parameters $z_1,\ldots,z_d$ with $I=(z_1,\ldots,z_c)$. The parameter quotient theorem gives $s=d-c$; comparing with $d=s+r$ gives $c=r$. The images of $z_1,\ldots,z_c$ form a basis of $I/\mathfrak m_AI$: they span, and their independence follows from independence in $\mathfrak m_A/\mathfrak m_A^2$, since $\mathfrak m_AI\subseteq\mathfrak m_A^2$. Thus step 3 gives $n=c=r$. The generators $p_i$ give a surjection $\mathbf Z^r\to P^{\mathrm{gp}}$. After tensoring with $\mathbf Q$ it is a surjection between vector spaces of dimension $r$, hence injective. Its integral kernel is therefore zero. Since $P$ is integral and generated by these $p_i$, the induced surjection $\mathbf N^r\to P$ is an isomorphism. This includes $r=0$.

source.place: VI, 1.7, printed p. 70, regular implies free: expand the regular-quotient and monoidal-ideal argument rather than invoking the conclusion as a new lemma.

proof.text: Conversely suppose $P\cong\mathbf N^r$ and let $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ be the images of its basis under a sharp chart. Then $I=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)$. Lift a regular system of $s$ parameters of $A/I$ to $b_1,\ldots,b_s\in\mathfrak m_A$. The list $(t_1,\ldots,t_r,b_1,\ldots,b_s)$ generates $\mathfrak m_A$: reduce any element modulo $I$, express it using the $b_j$, and subtract that expression to land in $I$. Its length $r+s$ equals $\dim A$. Consequently $A$ is regular, and this list is a regular system of parameters. The dimension bound for any set of maximal-ideal generators ensures it is minimal. In particular the $t_i$ are distinct members of such a system.

source.place: VI, 1.2, 1.6 and 1.7, printed pp. 69--70, free implies regular: generators and the log regular dimension formula.

proof.text: Regularity is unchanged by strict henselization, so steps 4 and 5 give precisely $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ regular if and only if $\overline M_{\bar x}\cong\mathbf N^r$. If this holds everywhere then every ordinary local ring of $X$ is regular. Since $X$ is locally Noetherian, the local-ring characterization of regular schemes gives regularity of $X$.

source.place: VI, 1.7, printed p. 70; pass between strict local rings and ordinary local rings.

proof.text: Under the everywhere-free hypothesis choose at each point a sharp chart $\mathbf N^r\to M|_W$ on an affine etale neighbourhood as in step 1, and write $t_i$ for its structural functions. The triviality locus in $W$ is exactly $D(f)$ with $f=\prod_{i=1}^r t_i$: the associated log structure is trivial precisely when every basis image is invertible. At any geometric point of $W$, a product of basis images is a unit exactly when each factor in its support is a unit. Thus its characteristic is $\mathbf N^J$, where $J$ indexes the nonunit $t_i$ at that point. Strict local rings of a pointed etale neighbourhood identify with those of the base, so log regularity pulls back to $W$. Applying step 5 at this point shows that these nonunit $t_i$ extend to parameters in the strict local ring. The chart neighbourhoods are locally Noetherian by the sharp-chart lemma.

source.place: VI, 1.6--1.7, printed p. 70; free charts describe the triviality locus and all their characteristic stalks.

proof.text: Let $B=\mathcal O_{W,w}$ and $A=B^{\mathrm{sh}}$ at a point of such a chart. By strict-henselization invariance, $B$ is regular. The canonical cotangent-space base-change isomorphism shows that the classes of the nonunit $t_i$ are linearly independent in $\mathfrak m_B/\mathfrak m_B^2$, since they are independent after extending scalars to the separable residue closure. Extend them to a basis of that cotangent space and lift the additional basis vectors to $B$. Nakayama says that this list generates $\mathfrak m_B$; its size is $\dim B$ by regularity (minimality follows from the dimension bound). It is therefore a regular system of parameters of $B$. This proves the claimed parameter assertion in ordinary local rings on an actual etale chart, not just in a formal completion.

source.place: VI, 1.7, printed p. 70; ordinary-local form of the parameter equations, using the cotangent-space comparison for strict henselization.

proof.text: In $B$, each nonunit $t_i$ is prime: permute a full parameter system to put it first; the parameter quotient theorem makes $B/(t_i)$ regular local, hence a domain. Different such $t_i$ do not divide one another: divisibility by a unit coefficient would make their cotangent classes dependent, and divisibility by a nonunit coefficient would put one in $\mathfrak m_B^2$. Since $B$ is a domain, their product is a non-zero-divisor. Moreover $(\prod_{i\in J}t_i)=\bigcap_{i\in J}(t_i)$: successively use primality and nondivisibility to divide an element of the intersection by each factor. The intersection is radical, so the product defines a reduced subscheme. Unit factors in $f$ do not change its ideal. For $J=\varnothing$, $f$ is a unit and the closed subscheme is empty.

source.place: VI, 1.7, printed p. 70; spell out reducedness and the non-zero-divisor property of the normal crossings equation.

proof.text: Thus on each chart $W$ the closed subscheme $V(f)$ is reduced and is an effective Cartier divisor. Indeed its quotient local rings are reduced by step 9, and multiplication by $f$ is injective on all local rings; equivalently its kernel sheaf vanishes. Its support is $W\setminus U$. Etale maps are flat and locally of finite presentation, hence open by the flat-lfp openness theorem. Since $U$ is the union of the open images of the chart opens $D(f)$, it is open in $X$, so $Z=X\setminus U$ is closed. The etale reduced-Cartier descent lemma identifies $V(f)$ with $Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times_XW$ and descends the effective Cartier property to $D=Z_{\mathrm{red}}$. The equations in step 8 are products of distinct members of parameter systems, as required for a normal crossings divisor. No assertion of distinct global irreducible components is used.

source.place: VI, 1.7, printed p. 70, and VIII, 3.4.4 and 4.1.1, printed pp. 110 and 117; descend the reduced local parameter equations.

proof.text: Finally $U$ is dense. Otherwise a nonempty open $V$ lies in $D$. Shrink to a nonempty affine open $\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq V$ on which the Cartier ideal is $(g)$, with $g$ a non-zero-divisor. Choose a point corresponding to a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $C$. Its local ring $B=C_{\mathfrak p}$ is regular, hence a nonzero domain. The element $g/1$ is nonzero, because multiplication by it is injective in this nonzero ring. The inverse image of the prime $(0)\subset B$ is therefore a prime of $C$ not containing $g$. This gives a point of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ outside $D$, contradicting $\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq V\subseteq D$. The empty scheme and empty boundary cause no exception; for $r=0$ the chart equation is the empty product $1$.

source.place: VI, 1.4 and 1.7, printed pp. 69--70; elementary density argument from the Cartier local equations.

proof_origin.place: Expose VI, 1.2, 1.6--1.7 and VIII, Lemma 3.4.3. Agent expansion using the monoidal-ideal correspondence and the regular-local quotient criterion; the source states the criterion but cites Niziol for its proof.
